title: RNARL: reinforcement learning-driven unified generative framework for multi-objective RNA codon design.
data_url: https://github.com/SII-ShenggengLin/RNARL (code + example_data) ; https://zenodo.org/records/17212245 (code zip, 912 KB, MIT)

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded the Zenodo code archive (912 KB, MIT licence) and opened all three data files it contains: example_train.csv, example_val.csv, example_test.csv. Each has exactly 9 rows and 8 columns (Protein_ID, Protein_Sequence, Protein_Length, CDS_Sequence, CDS_Length, CDS_Structure, CDS_MFE, CDS_CAI), no missing values, no duplicate coding sequences. Printed the numeric values (for example CDS_MFE -423.1 with CDS_CAI 0.920 for RefSeq protein XP_054196038.1). Also listed the live GitHub tree (only the same three example files, no data directory), read the repository README, and pulled the paper's supplementary Word file (16.4 MB, partially truncated but its text extracted) to read Supplementary Tables S1-S3.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: All real dataset sizes come from Supplementary Table S2 only, not from any downloadable file: training/validation/test splits of 38,139/2,119/2,119 for human, 28,144/1,564/1,564 for Arabidopsis thaliana (thale cress), 3,764/209/210 for Escherichia coli, 10,382/577/577 for Penicillium chrysogenum (a mould), 1,720/96/96 for Thermococcus kodakarensis (an archaeon), 13,653/759/759 for Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (an alga) and 21,533/1,197/1,196 for human circular RNA. Genome Biology has only posted an accepted-manuscript stub, so the Methods and any data-availability statement are not public; Europe PMC has no full text and no PMCID, and the supplement contains no mention of a sequence source, folding software, clustering tool or data deposit.

a1_downloadable.note: FAIL, checked in the files. The only downloadable data is 27 rows of example coding sequences (9 per split) in the GitHub/Zenodo code archive. The datasets the paper is built on (38,139 human coding sequences plus six other species/RNA-type sets, Supplementary Table S2) are deposited nowhere I could find: no accession in Europe PMC, no repository hit on the DOI, no data link in the README or supplement, and the published article page carries no data-availability statement yet.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Technically passes: CDS_MFE and CDS_CAI are real columns in the example CSV files. But for any usable number of rows the columns would have to be regenerated by running a folding program and a codon-usage calculation, i.e. constructed.

a3_inputs_present.note: Checked in the files: full protein sequences and full coding (RNA) sequences are present as text, no accession lookups needed.

a4_units_stated.note: Partly checked. CDS_CAI is a 0-1 index (values 0.70-0.95 observed) and CDS_MFE is clearly free energy in kcal/mol (-267 to -1629 for 432-1929 nucleotide sequences), but the unit is never written down in the files or the README.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL, counted in the files: 9 rows in each of example_train.csv, example_val.csv and example_test.csv, 27 labelled rows in total, against a checklist floor of about 1,500.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: <1 MB of released data; a rebuilt human set would be roughly 100-300 MB of sequence text
a6_fits_laptop.note: FAIL for reproducing the paper: the README's own hardware recommendation is two NVIDIA A100 80 GB graphics cards, 32 CPU cores and 256 GB of memory, and the generator embeds ESM-2 650M, a protein language model. A small surrogate predictor would fit a laptop, but the published framework does not.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: FAIL in the sense that it cannot be checked: Supplementary Table S2 claims tens of thousands of sequences per species, the download contains 27 rows, and there is no third source to adjudicate because no full text or deposit exists.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAIL, and this is the decisive one, verified in the files. Both targets are deterministic functions of the input sequence: CDS_CAI (codon adaptation index) is computed from the coding sequence plus a species codon-usage table, and CDS_MFE (minimum free energy) is computed by folding that same sequence (the file even ships the computed CDS_Structure dot-bracket string alongside it). Nothing here is a physical measurement of protein output, translation rate or stability, so a model fitted to these columns is a fast surrogate for existing software, not a model of biology.

existing_models.name: CodonTransformer (Fallahpour et al., Nature Communications 2025), a transformer that rewrites a protein into a species-tuned coding sequence
existing_models.score_and_split: Weights and training data on Hugging Face (adibvafa/CodonTransformer) and code on GitHub; trained on >1 million DNA-protein pairs from 164 organisms and evaluated with codon adaptation index and codon similarity index. I retrieved the repository, dataset and journal pages but did not read a split-level number.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not read; I retrieved listing pages only, so I am not quoting a discussion sentence.

existing_models.name: CodonBERT (Li et al., Genome Research 2024, Sanofi), a codon-level language model for mRNA
existing_models.score_and_split: Code and PyTorch weights in the Sanofi-Public/CodonBERT GitHub repository; reported as first or second on six of seven benchmark tasks, including a Sanofi influenza haemagglutinin mRNA expression set measured in HeLa cells, against TF-IDF, TextCNN, Codon2vec, RNABERT and RNA-FM. Numbers from the retrieved summary, not from the tables.

existing_models.name: RiboDecode (Nature Communications 2025, doi 10.1038/s41467-025-64894-x), a generative model for mRNA codon sequences validated on translation and therapeutic efficacy
existing_models.score_and_split: Retrieved the article listing only; it reports improved translation efficiency for vaccines and protein-replacement therapy, with experimental follow-up. No split-level number read.

existing_models.name: DeepCodon (Biosafety and Bioresearch/ScienceDirect 2025), a codon optimiser that preserves rare-codon clusters
existing_models.score_and_split: Retrieved listing only: trained on 1.5 million natural Enterobacteriaceae sequences then fine-tuned on highly expressed genes, reporting better in-silico host-preference metrics.

existing_models.name: COformer (PMC 2025), a convolution-plus-transformer codon optimiser for human cells, and CodonRL (PMC 2025), reinforcement learning with demonstration guidance for codon optimisation
existing_models.score_and_split: Retrieved listings only; CodonRL in particular is a near-identical reinforcement-learning formulation of the same task, published before RNARL.

backbone.name: ESM-2 650M (protein language model), which RNARL itself uses as the protein encoder; RNA-FM or CodonBERT would be the obvious encoders for the coding-sequence side
backbone.hardware: Freeze-and-head on cached embeddings would run on a 16 GB laptop CPU, but computing ESM-2 650M embeddings for tens of thousands of proteins is a 10-20 hour one-off; training RNARL as published needs two A100 graphics cards per its README.
backbone.licence: ESM-2 is MIT; RNARL code is MIT; the article text is Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0.

integration.partner_dataset: RefSeq/NCBI protein and coding sequences (the Protein_ID column holds RefSeq accessions such as XP_054196038.1 and NP_001268361.1), plus measured mRNA expression sets such as the Sanofi influenza haemagglutinin set released with CodonBERT or Human Protein Atlas expression
integration.join_key: RefSeq protein accession, which maps to UniProt and Ensembl
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do the computed quantities this framework optimises (codon adaptation index and folding free energy) actually predict measured protein output, or are published codon optimisers competing on proxies nobody has shown to matter? That is a good question, but answering it needs the measured expression data, which this paper does not contain.

controls.positive_control: Available in principle and trivially: predict sequence length or GC content from the coding sequence, which any working pipeline must nail. Also, codon adaptation index itself is recomputable exactly, so a surrogate model's error is measurable against ground truth software.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling and feature ablation are runnable, but they are weak here because the label is a deterministic function of the features, so leakage is the design rather than a risk.
controls.external_validation: None in this paper. Any honest external check would need measured expression (for example the Sanofi influenza haemagglutinin mRNA set distributed with CodonBERT), which is a different dataset entirely.

honest_claim_h3: With what is actually downloadable, the only honest claim is: a neural network can reproduce the codon adaptation index and folding free energy that existing software computes exactly from the same sequence, for 27 released human coding sequences. Nothing about protein output or vaccine performance is claimable.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a protein sequence to generate a coding sequence scored for codon usage and folding stability.
plain_idea.train_on: Protein sequence plus its natural coding sequence, with two precomputed scores per row. Verified count: 27 rows (9 train, 9 validation, 9 test). The paper's own sets are 38,139 human rows and six other species/RNA-type sets, but those files are not released.
plain_idea.predict: Either a redesigned coding sequence, or the two scores. The 'true answer' is not a measurement: the codon adaptation index comes from arithmetic on a species codon-usage table and the free energy comes from running a folding algorithm on the very sequence being scored.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: The underlying question (which codon choices actually raise protein yield) matters to every mRNA vaccine and protein-production group, but it can only be answered with measured expression data, which this paper neither provides nor uses.

more_or_better_data.why: We would have 27 released rows against CodonTransformer's >1 million DNA-protein pairs across 164 organisms and CodonBERT's >10 million mRNA sequences. Even the paper's unreleased 38,139-row human set is far smaller.

confidence_score.why: There are no replicate measurements to estimate noise from, because there are no measurements at all; the two target columns are exact computations, so their 'noise' is zero by construction.

models_beatable.why: CodonTransformer (2025) and CodonBERT (2024) are both recent, both ship open weights and code, and CodonBERT was benchmarked against five alternatives on seven tasks including a measured HeLa-cell expression set. CodonRL already published the reinforcement-learning angle.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first and third conditions: there is no shared evaluation split to run the existing models on, and the quantity being fitted here is computed rather than measured, so no added data makes a prediction of it more biologically meaningful.

label_elsewhere.sources: Not applicable as a label: codon adaptation index and minimum free energy are not stored in resources, they are recomputed on demand by standard software for any sequence, so there is no external labelled set to validate against. The genuinely measured analogue (protein output per mRNA design) exists only in small assay sets, such as the influenza haemagglutinin expression data released with CodonBERT.
label_elsewhere.join_key: RefSeq protein accession (present in the Protein_ID column)
label_elsewhere.why: Because the target is free to compute exactly for any sequence, extra labelled data adds nothing; the scarce and valuable label would be measured expression, which this dataset lacks.

ml_idea: The project considered was to train a cheap surrogate that scores a candidate coding sequence for codon adaptation index and folding free energy directly from the protein plus codon choices, using frozen ESM-2 embeddings and a small head, then use it to rank redesigns. It is rejected because the targets are exactly computable from the input, the released data is 27 rows, and open recent models (CodonTransformer, CodonBERT, CodonRL) already occupy the task.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, nothing timed. Rebuilding the paper's human set would mean downloading RefSeq coding sequences, clustering proteins by identity and folding tens of thousands of sequences up to 3,900 nucleotides, where folding cost grows with the cube of length. ESM-2 650M on a laptop CPU runs at roughly 1-2 sequences per second, so about 15 hours for ~40,000 proteins. The published generator needs graphics cards per its own README.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows in the released example_data CSV files. I did: 9 per split, 27 total, versus 38,139 claimed for human in Supplementary Table S2. Then look at what the two target columns are: both are computed from the sequence in the same row.

verdict_reason: Part A fails three ways, all verified in the files. A8: both targets (codon adaptation index and minimum free energy) are deterministic computations on the input sequence, with the folded structure shipped in the same table, so any model is a surrogate for free software rather than a model of biology, and no measured expression or translation value appears anywhere. A5/A1: the only downloadable data is 27 example rows; the 38,139-row human set and the six other species/RNA-type sets named in Supplementary Table S2 are deposited nowhere, and Genome Biology has published only an accepted-manuscript stub with no data-availability statement. A6: the authors' own hardware requirement is two A100 80 GB graphics cards with 256 GB of memory. On top of that, the field is served by recent open models with weights and code (CodonTransformer, CodonBERT) and CodonRL already published the reinforcement-learning formulation.
